div.p:
PLAIN TALK
Four Lives from Orange County, New York
Interviews edited by Kay Kenny

Before I was married, I worked in an ice-cream store in Highland
Falls. I was lucky to get the job. It helped: the extra money. My
father had retired. He had arthritis so bad and couldn’t work. I
worked in the ice-cream store all through high school. I had
every intention of being a nurse then, but money was hard to come
by. My mother said that if I wanted to go to college and be a
nurse, I would have to go out and make the money for it, but
working in an ice-cream store I wasn’t making that much. Then
I met my husband and being a nurse, why, that went down
the drain!

We went together for a
year and a half before we
were married. I had three
children. I had no intention
of going to work after I was
married. I was quite content
being at home. I always
liked the idea of keeping a
home and it's more or less
a tradition for the women in
my family to be homemak-
ers. My mother never worked
outside the house when we
were growing up, only
when my father retired and
couldn’t provide anything.
My daughter is a homemak-
er and my son's wife is
another one that likes to stay
home with the kids. My
youngest sister is the only
one that works. I don’t know
how she can do it, day in
and day out for so many
years!

My husband is of the idea
that a woman belongs in the
home. Whenever I would
say that I would like to get a
job, he would say, "You’ve
got enough to do here." He
never really liked the idea of me going out. I think he used to
feel that people would think he couldn’t support me. I used to
feel guilty about not going out to work. I don’t anymore. All of a
sudden there was this big surge: everybody was going out to
work. Someone would say, "Oh, you don’t work?"” and eyebrows
would go up. But I enjoy being at home. I always got a pleasure
in washing and ironing and seeing things clean.

You still have some people who think: "Well, what do you do all
day, you don’t go out to business?” They think you don’t do
anything, but you get involved in a lot of other things. When a
neighbor calls and says she needs you, you drop everything
and go. I was involved in a lot of volunteer work when the kids
were growing up.

If I had to go out to work right now, I really don’t know what I
would do. I don’t know if my volunteer work would put me in
any particular job; maybe a salesgirl, I don’t know. Most of my
friends are homemakers and I haven’t noticed a lot of them
going back to work. The big change has been with the younger

generation. My generation, we would think twice about going
out to work. Well, there probably wasn’t as great a need as now,
with the price of food and everything, but when I was first
married, I didn’t expect a house right away and all the new
furniture. I think young people now, they want a home right
away and all new furniture, two cars, the latest thing: everything.
It took a long time to get that in our generation. The war was
over there was a lot more money around. So, maybe it was the
way they were brought up. You have to admire them in a way.

But in another way, I don’t
admire that you have to have
everything right away. If you
have it all, what have you to
look forward to? I think
that’s why theyre more mis-
content. It’s probably our
generation that did it to
them so they can’t help it!

During the war, so many
women went out to work.
Sometimes they took over
men’s jobs because the men
weren’t there. I think it all
led to this "women's lib'
stuff, if that's what you want
to call it. You know, I don't
blame them in a lot of ways,
wanting to get paid if theyre
doing an equal job. A lot of
it I don’t agree with, a lot of
it I don’t even pay attention
to, but, I think that if a
woman does a good job
equal to a man’s job, she
should get paid as much. I
don’t see wanting the re¬
sponsibility of being over a
lot of men: l’m sure they
must resent it. I wouldn't
want to do it myself. Well,
everybodys different. Some
women have that drive to get to the top.

Now, I do think that men put women down. It’s just an attitude;
I can’t put my finger on it, but you sense it. l’m sure it has
changed some. It’s bound to. The women are changing it with
all their drives and meetings and such. Not being out in the
business world, I wouldn’t experience that change much though.

But, I think that if women have children, they lose a lot when
they go out to work. I can remember my kids used to say, "Boy,
Mom, it’s good to come in. You can smell something cooking
and know you’re here." If women really feel that they want to get
out of the house and do something, if it makes them happy
—fine! Maybe they figure they want everything right away instead
of waiting and saving for it the way we had to do. But, I think
there’s a lot of women who go out to business who would rather
be home. Sometimes it’s a necessity, but sometimes, let’s face
it, some women are just not made to be homemakers.

Kay Kenny is a visual artist. "Plain Talk" emerged out of her
work in upstate New York, surveying women’s employment prob-
lems in Orange County.

I have always made five goals for what I wanted to do in my life.
I wanted to get married and have children. I always loved
make-up and hair-cutting; I wanted to work as a cosmetologist
in some kind of make-up field. I wanted to go to college and be
a nurse and I wanted to go to college to write a book. l’ve only
nursing and my book left, which l’ve started to write. l’ve just
turned the age where the book will be about my past: my
teenagehood.

l’m twenty years old. I have two daughters, one four and one
who is six months old. I was fifteen when I left high school and
was married. I was in school three weeks of my tenth grade year
and I had gotten pregnant. My parents told me it was my decision
what I wanted to do. My boyfriend was nineteen-at the time and
working. He said, "I want to get married. We can make it work."
We did and here I am and that’s that!

My husband’s a really homebound person. He’s the father type
person. He runs my whole house. When I was seventeen he
bought me a house for our
second anniversary. He
comes home from work,
expects his dinner, his home
spotless, his children wait¬
ing for him. He’Il say "Fran,
Ireally don’t want you to do
this." or "I don’t want you
to do that." or "You’re
pushing yourself too hard.
But he would never give me
a direct, "No, you can’t do
this." We sit and talk a lot
and it's "Will you help me?
I need your help." That type
of thing. He watches my
children whenever I have
things to do and he's
rebuilding my house now.
It's our house but it's more
mine because l’m always in
it. I take care of it.

My husband’s a mechanic
at J.C.Penneys up in Mid¬
dletown. He wants to open
his own business, maybe
go into a family type deal
because his brother does
all the auto body and my
husband does everything
from rebuilding cars to... everything! They want to open up a
shop and I would take care of the books. I told him, "I can
handle all your books. My mother’s an accountant. She could
show me." I would help him as far as that goes, but l’m not the
kind of person who would hang around there. I said, "TII pick
up the books, but it’s your business. I’II just help you.'

My mother’s very young; she married very young. My sister’s 21
and l’m 20 and the three of us have a good time when we go out.
We do things together. People can’t believe that we’re mother
and daughters and when they hear that there are grandchildren
—it completely blows their minds! My mother’s a public
accountant for a public relations firm. She controls a whole
office. My father lives in Florida. He’s an auto mechanic. He
owns his own business. My parents got divorced when I was
10. Under the circumstances, we didn’t see him after that. I
guess the problem was that my father was just an auto¬
mechanic and my mother was working in a big company. She
would have to go to these big conventions and things. He
couldn’t relate to them. He never wanted her to work, whether

they needed the extra money or not. He knew she was going up
and he was at a standstill. She’s worked for her company for
years, ever since she was old enough to get in there. She was
a hard worker. She picked things up pretty quick. She read a
lot of books. Her biggest dream in life was to be Somebody and
to make good money. She did and she wasn’t going to let any¬
thing stand in her way because she knew she could do it.

My mother-in-law is homebound. If my father-in-law can’t earn
it, they do without because he’s the Man-of-the-House. She
goes right along with it. She’d like me to stay home. That’s how
they believe: a woman should not work. It’s weird; they’re just
different people with different beliefs. I tell them, "When I have
this big beautiful house and me and Kenny have a lot of money
because we’ve worked at it together...." they look at me like l’m
a nut! They say that everything I want, I don’t care what I have
to do, I get it. That’s just how I am! I will WORK for something!
I don’t believe in going to W.T.Grants to buy clothes, that type
of stuff. l’m different. I guess because I wasn’t brought up on
that. I took my first daughter
to buy a coat. It was about
S55. I liked the coat, and
you know, you get what you
pay for. Well, they thought I
was sick! I said, "But it's a
good coat; she’ll stay warm."
They said, "She doesn’t need
that; buy her something
cheaper." I can’t do that.

Right now, I deal with Mary
Kay Cosmetics. I hold skin
care classes and offer pri¬
vate beauty I
love it! I learned about Mary
Kay when I was going to
BOCES, studying to be a
cosmetologist. When I fi¬
nally turned 18 I decided
that this was something I
really wanted to do. You
can do it when you want to
do it. You work your time
around your family which
is nice; not too many jobs
let you do that.

A man can’t always think
the woman’s place is in the
home. They can’t! They have
to be involved with their own needs. My needs are just fulfilling
myself. I have a baby 6 months old. As soon as she starts
school, I will attend college for nursing. It’s something that I
would like to know, just for the knowledge of it. It’s self-
fulfilling for me. I don’t even know if I would stop at nursing;
maybe I would move on to a doctor or something. I don’t know!

I’m young. I have a long time to fullfill everything that I really
want to do. l’m very prepared for anything. I know I can do
anything. I plan my whole day. I get up at 5:30, get my
husband’s breakfast, get his shower ready, get my husband up.
Kids get up, I feed them, take care of them. My housework's
done. By 9:00 I go and do what I have to do, take care of
business, and by 4:00 I know it’s time to go home and cook: we
eat when he comes home. If I have a show to do, it’s usually
around 8:00. Finally, the kids are in bed by 7:00 and we can
relax. I have a little bit of time to talk with him, then I go do
what I have to do. I come home at a reasonable time and go to
bed and get up the next day and start all over again. I have
everything in hand.

l’Il be 40 May 10th, if I live to see it. I left Virginia when I was 4
and went to school in Newburgh, N.Y. I stopped in 10th grade
’cause my mother had too many kids in school and she said she
couldn’t give me the type of clothes like a high-school girl
should have. My father had 21 children. There’s 18 of us living,
but he’s been married three times. Only my mother’s kids were
living at home. She had 12.

I was the oldest girl, yeah.... listen, I had to give them their
bath, make sure they got their homework. I had to get up at
5AM to get breakfast ready, then I had to pack their lunches
and get the kids out to school. Then I had to go to work at
Dupex Bags. I was only making $30 a week but I had to turn
over half of that every time. I remember one time I talked back
to Daddy ’cause he told me to give my mother one half and him
the other half. I told him, "Well, it’s no use me working."

My father worked in a junkyard down by the Hudson River. I
never had no life at home, really, because: well, my father used
to make me take all my
clothes off and he'd whip
me with switches he got
down at the river. I called
them tree branches ’cause
that’s what they seemed like
to me. I was striped like a
tiger all the way up and I
was just coming into wo-
manhood—June apples—I
have much more than that
now. I was bloody every-
where he hit me: nothing
but welts.

One time I had to stay
home from high school for
two weeks ’cause he slapped
me and all five fingers was
on my face. I asked my
mother if he was my real
father. I got to the point
where I threatened to com¬
mit suicide. I was gonna
take any pill I saw lying
around. Finally, I called
Family Services and my
mother agreed to let me live
with my godmother. When
the cops came to pick me
up, Daddy pulled a gun on
them. He said, "Nobody
tells me how to raise my kids!"

I think about my father a lot. I think the reason I don’t have any
kids is that he could have damaged my female organs. I said on
many days that l’Il be glad when he dies and, you’d better be¬
lieve, when he died I really didn’t take it too hard.

Anyway, when I was 16 I went to live with my godmother in
Pennsylvania. I had a janitor’s job at Westinghouse. I had to lift
those heavy buckets and those mops and stuff—I wasn’t
supposed to be doing that kind of work. I have syncopy so I get
seizures and dizzy spells. The doctor told me they come from
anxiety. After 6 or 8 months at Westinghouse I was terminated.
Every job l’ve ever had, I was terminated.

When I was in Pennsylvania, I paid §20 and I took a
high-school test. It took three nights. Some of the girls who
took it had just got out of school and they missed by more
points than I did. I was really amazed at myself, ’cause I only
missed it by 12 points. l’m gonna take another one if welfare
pays for it.

I was 24 when I got married, but I never had no life with my
husband, really. He first started me drinking. We separated after
20 years and that was one of the reasons. I mean, it’s all very in¬
teresting, the things people tell what they do under the influence
of alcohol. It’s really ridiculous: they get in jail and then they don’t
remember nothing about it. I ain’t never been that far to extremes.

I used to go to the mental health clinic. The doctor knows more
than I do. He seemed to think that I didn’t need to come there
anymore, so I didn’t go back. I guess he just got tired.

Right now, l’m not working, and, let me tell you, the welfare in
Newburgh is really nasty. I want to work, but I can’t go working
in places for six months and then get sick and welfare knows
that. I get to thinking about how I didn’t get no education. l’m
not hard to catch on to things, but what can I do? Every job you
see in the papers you need experience, but if you don’t have the
training you don’t get the experience. The only work I do now is
when my uncle moves stuff—sometimes he asks me to help
him. There’s something about it I don’t like, but it keeps me
from staying in the house
all day, looking at the win¬
dows and the walls. I feel
much more relaxed. Right
now, l’m waiting to hear to
get on SSI. I sit here worry-
ing every day, watching for
the mailman. I’m scared
somebody will steal my
mail.
Gladys Canning

’Course, I never go no
place unless it’s shopping,
to the wash, or something. I
quess becausethere's some¬
thing that's in me now that
don’t bother about going
nowhere. Since I started
attending A.A. meetings it's
really good, but the meet¬
ings didn’t start till 9 pm,
so Miss Taylor started hav¬
ing them at noon. I asked
her to ’cause I get scared a
lot of the time, walking at
night by myself. When I
was 24, I got raped and that
is something l’II never get
over. The judge—and he
ain't nothing either—he
says, "All you had to do
was cross your legs and he
couldn’t have raped you.” But the man was very violent. He
pulled me into the car and wrang my wrists and stuff. I couldn’t
get out of the car ’cause he didn’t stop at no red lights. I looked
around for something to hit him with in the car, but I couldn’t
find nothing. It was a terrible experience. When I got home, I
called the police. A detective came and made me get out of the
bathtub so I could identify the man. We had to put so much
pressure on the judge, but finally they locked him up, after me
and my sister went to the pastor and got some aid from him and
some of his members. For about four years I felt very unclean,
no matter how much I washed.

As far as life goes, I didn’t have too much, but I was always
the type of person to help people; I really like to do that. I don’t
have many visitors. If Miss Taylor at the A.A. had a bigger
place, maybe I could meet more people, but very seldom do I
see another woman there. I tried to get one of my girlfriends to
go but she didn’t give a damn one way or another. If we had a
bigger place, Miss Taylor said, we could help kids to plant
seeds, or somebody could teach sewing or whatever they know.
But what are we going to do now? We barely have room to walk.

I was very fortunate because my mother and my aunt were both
singers and my grandfather was a ballroom dancer, so they
started my training very early: when I was about four. I went to
Professor O’Brien’s Normal School of Dancing. It was 6 days a
week. We had Interpretive on Monday, Egyptian on Tuesday,
Spanish on Wednesday, acrobatics on Thursday tap on Friday
and ballet on Saturday. It was a very rich and very esoteric
education because the teacher was very classical. We all wore
tunics and on Egyptian night we came out of mummy cages. I
went there during my most formative years: 5 years with Professor
O’Brien and his wife at the piano.

Nobody said anything about a career, but I performed at an
early age with my mother and my aunt. My mother started taking
singing lessons when I was born—as an outlet. She worked for
ten years professionally after that. She loved jazz, so it was her
influence that got me into it. She was a very soulful person. Of
course, my father worked 16 hours a day and was never home,
so that I could get such a good education. He was a very dog¬
matic Italian father. Yet, even though he was very old-fashioned,
it was always as if I were ex¬
pected to be independent. It
was never any question of
saying: "Well, when you
grow up you’ll get married
and you won’t need all this."
The tradition of the females
in my family was very
strong: they were all work-
ers. However, nobody ever
wants their son or daughter
to go into show business,
even if theyre in it them¬
selves. Theyre always hop-
ing you'll turn into an
historian or something, sol
was never guided.

Iwas 15 when my parents
got divorced. I was going to
Alice Duffys, who had a
very typical dance school
—much more expensive,
but very good! My mother's
agent came to one of the
recitals and said, "She's
had enough of this teacher.
He sent me to Stanley
Brown’s in Boston. I would
go into Boston to study
every day after school. I
never got much of an educa¬
tion, obviously, of any intellectual type. I mean, I was 15 in
Boston, hanging around—I was fortunate enough to meet a
group of college people. We would go and talk in Hayes and
Bickfords and they kinda accepted me as a mascot—a kooky
mascot with dyed red hair and black eyes: the odd one. So I
was getting educated.

By the time I was married, I already had a thorough education
in dance and music, not an intellectual one, but in those days
people didn’t talk about dance like they do now. If you had
talent, you did it.

Dance is so strenuous, it’s so hard, that I didn’t feel much
competition with men or much argument until I was married
In fact, other than the sexual problem of being pursued everytime
I turned around, I wouldn’t say that I was influenced or tied up
in the whole thing of feeling female, or what that meant or that I
had problems. I would have a hell of a lot of problems when I
would go into a producer’s or director’s office. That was awful!
That was a nightmare! And continually a nightmare! I would
become evil! Evil! And the more evil I got, the more lecherous
they got! Some gals have wonderful techniques that I learned

too late, of complete ingenuousness and naivete. Even though
they might be the raunchiest people in the world, when they
walked in there they didn’t know a thing. l’d go in there and l’d
say "OK baby, I dare ya! Go ahead!" Well, needless to say, they
did! That was terrible! In those days I was very voluptuous. I
looked like they should come on to me. It’s very unfortunate
that your physical type should demand that kind of response. It
was appalling, humiliating and awful.

I was afraid of the hard shell I needed to form, the ag¬
gressiveness, but I was also afraid of being made into something
I wasn’t. I mean, when you’re in this business, you’re a
commodity. I had managers that would decide who I would be.
One manager had the idea that would be a combination of Carol
Channing, Marcel Marceau and Charlie Chaplin. I got sent to
the hairdressers and I got dressed a certain way, had to go out
with certain people and couldn’t hang out in the jazz joints that
I always did. I got a contract to sign for MGM, but I was supposed
to play, you know, tootsies under the table before I could sign
the contract. I became a very distorted creature. It was a desper
ateness and a real desolat¬
edness and I wasn’t an ex¬
pert at taking care of myself.
I lived too hard.

I never wanted to get
married. I never saw myself
in that position. My career
had really been snowball
ing, but it also had a tre¬
mendous amount of hard
knocks: it was a very vicious
profession. I was getting a
little evil and paranoid and
I didn’t like myself too
much. I was at a low ebb. A
man came along and said,
"TII take care of you, be¬
cause if I don’t, you’ll die.
Well, I believed it!

He was an artist, a paint¬
er. We had children right
away and moved to the
country, and led a very crea¬
tive life. Four years after I
got married, I went back to
dancing under great duress.
It was never really possible
to dance when I was mar-
ried. I would get terrible
migraines because the has¬
sle at home was so great. I
did start working with a composer, doing avant-garde things. I
enjoyed what I did with him very much. We did some good
work, but I wasn’t having a career. I was home with my children,
farming, loading manure, feeding the pigs and watching my
husband paint. He really made a point that I couldn’t bring
money into the house. I’d make §25 and he’d say, "Well, I can
make S25 in five minutes. It takes you three days, so why bother!"
I didn’t think that, well, l’m making that now, later l’II make a lit-
tle more. I accepted that small position, saying that it’s true. Yet,
we led a very interesting life—insulated but interesting. I don’t
resent it for a minute. I think I would have, if, when we got di¬
vorced, I hadn’t had all those years of training and found myself
with nothing. I did have my career before. I had something!

I never in my wildest dreams thought of picking up my career
again, or ever thought I wasn’t at the end of it. I was 34—35,
that, for a dancer is old. The things that have opened up and
what life has taught me since, have shocked me so much I still
can’t believe it! I finally feel strong enough to deal with that
push-pull foxtrot affair with success. I wouldn’t be gobbled up.
I do feel that my time has come. l’m definitely on that plane.
